Fermanagh
fur-MAN-uh
n. (the Ulster county of the Maguires and the lakes, whose town of Enniskillen held out for William in 1689)
Irish Fear Manach, the men of Manach, a population group name; the county is dominated by Upper and Lower Lough Erne.

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

Fermanagh is the Ulster county of Lough Erne, a country of water and drumlins that was the lordship of the Maguires until the Plantation, when it was divided among English and Scottish undertakers and the town of Enniskillen was laid out on its island site between the two lakes. Its moment came in 1689. When James II's Irish army moved north, Enniskillen and Derry were the two Protestant places that did not submit; the Enniskillen men, under Gustavus Hamilton and the rector William Smyth, armed themselves, raised horse and foot, and operated offensively through the summer, defeating a much larger force under Mountcashel at Newtownbutler in July and so relieving the pressure on Derry. William Bedell, the best bishop the Irish establishment produced, had held the neighbouring see of Kilmore from 1629, learned Irish, preached in it and had the Old Testament translated. The dictionary records the defence and then names the thing the entry exists to name, which is the conversion of a deliverance into a permanent identity.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines a bulwark as a bastion or rampart; a garrison as a body of troops in a fortress; to besiege as to surround with an army; a tower as a lofty building; and deliverance as rescue.

expand to see more

BULWARK, n. A bastion; a rampart; a mound of earth or other matter raised for defence.

GARRISON, n. A body of troops stationed in a fort or fortified town for its defence.

BESIEGE, v.t. To lay siege to; to surround with armed forces; to beset with a view to compel surrender.

TOWER, n. A building, either round or square, raised to a considerable elevation; a fortress.

DELIVERANCE, n. Release from captivity, slavery, oppression or any restraint; rescue from danger.

Key Scripture

Isa 26:1 — "In that day shall this song be sung in the land of Judah; We have a strong city; salvation will God appoint for walls and bulwarks."

Pro 18:10 — "The name of the LORD is a strong tower: the righteous runneth into it, and is safe."

Psa 20:7 — "Some trust in chariots, and some in horses: but we will remember the name of the LORD our God."

Heb 11:10 — "For he looked for a city which hath foundations, whose builder and maker is God."

Modern Corruption

Ulster county of Lough Erne and the Maguires, planted after 1609, whose town of Enniskillen armed itself in 1689 and beat Mountcashel at Newtownbutler in July, relieving the pressure on Derry.

expand to see more

The corruption to name is the one Ulster has been most damaged by, and the dictionary names it as a misuse of a real mercy. Enniskillen in 1689 was a genuine deliverance: a small Protestant population, expecting massacre, armed itself and was preserved. What was afterwards done with that memory is another matter. A deliverance commemorated annually becomes a founding story, a founding story becomes an identity, and an identity sanctifies a politics; the siege is then no longer something God did but something a community is. Scripture allows the gladness and relocates the walls. Isaiah's song is sung about a city whose defence is not its masonry: “We have a strong city; salvation will God appoint for walls and bulwarks” (Isa 26:1), and the only tower a man may run into is a name: “The name of the LORD is a strong tower: the righteous runneth into it, and is safe” (Pro 18:10).

The second paragraph names the alternative that was available in the same county and was not followed. William Bedell held Kilmore from 1629, learned Irish in middle age, required his clergy to use it, preached to Irish-speaking congregations and procured the translation of the Old Testament; when the rising came in 1641 the Irish of his diocese protected him and gave him an honourable burial. That is the other way a Protestant minority might have lived in Ireland, and it was tried and it worked. Against the trust that armed men place in their own numbers the psalmist sets the only safe memory: “Some trust in chariots, and some in horses: but we will remember the name of the LORD our God” (Psa 20:7). And the city a believer is finally told to look for is not any of these, since Abraham “looked for a city which hath foundations, whose builder and maker is God” (Heb 11:10).

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew chomah (H2346), a wall; Hebrew migdal (H4026), a tower; Greek themelios (G2310), a foundation.

expand to see more

Hebrew chomah (H2346) — a wall, a rampart; “salvation will God appoint for walls and bulwarks”, Isaiah 26:1.

Hebrew 'oz (H5797) — strength, might; “The name of the LORD is a strong tower”, Proverbs 18:10.

Hebrew migdal (H4026) — a tower, a raised stronghold; “is a strong tower: the righteous runneth into it”, Proverbs 18:10.

Hebrew rekeb (H7393) — a chariot, a team; “Some trust in chariots, and some in horses”, Psalm 20:7.

Greek themelios (G2310) — a foundation, something laid down; “a city which hath foundations”, Hebrews 11:10.

Usage

"“We have a strong city” (Isa 26:1) — Newtownbutler, July 1689."

"“The name of the LORD is a strong tower” (Pro 18:10) — the only tower a man may run into."

"“whose builder and maker is God” (Heb 11:10) — against a deliverance made into an identity."
